title: Proximity search for 0-1 mixed-integer convex programming
contribution: A general-purpose primal heuristic (proximity search) with three CPLEX implementations and an evaluation protocol for heuristics: impose a cutoff f(x) <= f(x̃) − θ and minimise the Hamming distance to x̃ instead of the original objective.
problem_entry: Best-bound search is weak at early good solutions (p. 2); entry: add the cutoff f(x) ≤ f(x̃) − θ, then the objective is free, so minimise Δ(x, x̃) and let the black-box solver make primal moves (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Change the sub-MIP's objective, not its constraints; f and Δ swap roles relative to local branching (pp. 3, 7); 'improved relaxation grip' for small θ (Table 1, pp. 5-6; Table 2, pp. 7-8).
assumptions: 0-1 MIP with convex f, g (convexity not strictly required), binaries only in Δ, first feasible solution assumed easy (pp. 1-2, 4, 6); 130 instances: set covering, SNDlib network design, ramp-loss SVM (pp. 12-14).
proof_devices: valid-bound remark: if infeasibility is proven for θ, f(x̃) − θ is a valid lower bound (p. 5)
experiments: CPLEX 12.4 single-thread, ten arms, same x̃ for all, primal integral at 5-1200 s plus pairwise 1%-better curves, column-generation re-optimisation test on 603 subinstances; no seeds or statistical tests (pp. 12-23).
positioning: Proximity term 'of course not new' (p. 6); read as a dual version of the authors' local branching and the feasibility pump (p. 7); differs from Bonami et al.'s MINLP pump (p. 8); RINS and polishing as benchmarks (p. 9).
writing: Framed as a computational investigation of pros and cons with proof-of-concept code (pp. 1, 3), recurring 'simple (and clean)' clause (pp. 3-5, 10-11), named mechanism (p. 5), self-reported adoption in CBC and GLPK (p. 23).
limits_future: Limits: hard cutoff θ, primal nature trapping in small improvements, binaries only (pp. 6, 23); future: hybrid with local branching and RINS, MIP-and-refine, proximity objective in pricing (p. 24).

method_links.note: the move from x̃ is handed to the black-box solver as a sub-MIP with a changed objective; recentering version runs CPLEX as a black box; minimal code; direct evidence for Heuristic 2 ('move one piece')

transferable: Proximity search: impose the cutoff f(x) ≤ f(x̃) − θ, minimise the Hamming distance to x̃, stop at the first feasible solution, recentre and repeat. Then re-optimise the continuous variables with the binaries fixed (pp. 4, 10).
Use a soft cutoff with slack z and objective Δ + Mz, so that the old incumbent serves as a warm start and the solver's RINS stays active. Stop with EPAGAP = M/2 (pp. 11, 15).
On one hard instance, tabulate the root-LP histogram, LP time and iterations against the parameter, for the new method and its rival (pp. 6, 8).
To compare heuristics, report the primal integral at several horizons together with pairwise "at least 1% better" probability curves (pp. 14, 17-19).

Build a re-optimisation test bed: an external column-generation driver creates nested subinstances independently of the heuristic under test, and every arm gets the same subinstance and warm start (pp. 21-22).

quotes.text: instead of modifying the constraints of the MIP at hand with the aim of reducing the search space, we modify the objective function with the aim of easing the search.

The good news is that even weak models (notably, those making extensive use of big-M tricks) can become effective when used within a proximity search framework, due to the improved relaxation grip induced by the proximity objective function.

title: Exploiting erraticism in search
contribution: A viewpoint that MIP erraticism should be exploited rather than averaged away, with the bet-and-run framework (short runs of diversified clones, then finish the most promising one) and a working default.
problem_entry: Erraticism is usually a drawback; the paper takes the opposite view, treating tree search as a chaotic amplifier (p. 1), drawing on SAT/CP restarts and racing ramp-up made sequential, with two questions: diversify and select (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Bet-and-run: solve the first LP, run C randomised clones for N nodes, pick the best and run it to the limit (Figure 1, p. 5); potential measured first with 100 seeds on 58 instances (Table 1, pp. 3-4); RAN0-RAN3 diversification (pp. 4-5).
assumptions: General MILP in equality form; RAN3 relies on dual degeneracy (pp. 2-5); 344 instances from COR@L and MIPLIB 2010 after listed exclusions; 58 medium instances for the preliminary study (pp. 3, 7).
proof_devices: optimal-face argument: RAN3's fixing of nonzero-reduced-cost nonbasics keeps the copy inside the optimal face (p. 4)
experiments: CPLEX 12.3 single-thread with dummy callback in every arm, 10,000 s limit, default vs bet-and-run plus ideal oracles, node classes blind to arm; losses on easy classes, −28.5% time on hard ones, +17.2% time overall; one run per instance per arm (pp. 6-12).
positioning: Credits Danna 2008 and MIPLIB 2010 (p. 1), SAT/CP restarts, backdoors, ParaSCIP racing (pp. 1-2); portfolios set aside to study pure erraticism (p. 2); credit-and-extend tone.
writing: Argued thesis ('we argue', p. 1), modest proof-of-concept frame (pp. 1, 6, 10), losses stated as expected and turned into an on/off usage rule (p. 8), one self-assessment (p. 8).
limits_future: Limits: unsophisticated selection rule (p. 6), gains overtaken by erraticism in the hardest class, overhead on easy instances (pp. 8-10), 148 unsolved instances outside evidence (p. 7); future: source-level diversification, learned selection, restarts reusing information, portfolios, NR on the fly (p. 10).

quotes.text: Erraticism is generally viewed as a drawback to be avoided. Instead, we argue that a certain degree of erraticism is unavoidable, as it is related to the exponential nature of tree search that acts as a chaotic amplifier, so one has to cope with it.
Therefore, one has to content him/herself with a criterion that gives a positive correlation between the selected run and those that a posteriori behave better than the average.

title: Boosting the feasibility pump
contribution: An algorithmic enhancement of the feasibility pump's rounding step: an integer line search that enumerates all roundings along an extended, bound-projected segment at modest cost.
problem_entry: FP improvements almost all target projection; the effort is 'lopsided' (pp. 2-3); entry: put effort into the rounding step and examine all roundings along a segment through x* (p. 3).
key_idea: Integer line search replacing rounding: efficient enumeration of roundings, cheap end points (conic combination of violated rows), extension and projection onto the bound box, timed propagation (pp. 3, 10-11, 18).
assumptions: General MIP with bounds; general integers via bound box; continuous variables need one warm-started LP per point (pp. 4, 8, 12-14); 1,304 instances from MIPLIB 2003/2010, COR@L, OR-LIB with 31 removed for stated reasons (p. 17).
proof_devices: breakpoint counting: breakpoints at λ̄ᵢ plus integer multiples of 1/(xᵗᵢ − xˢᵢ) (pp. 6-7)
pseudo-polynomial bound of Algorithm 2 in |xᵗ − xˢ|, then in |u − l| after filtering (pp. 8, 12, 14)
three-binary example for extension and projection (Figure 1, pp. 11-13)
experiments: Xeon 3.16 GHz, CPLEX (version not stated), shadow design along the FP+ trajectory, performance profiles of improvement over FP; FP+ls better on about 66% and rescues about 12%; matched-budget and random-direction attribution; no seeds or tests (pp. 17-24).
positioning: Inside the FP lineage and older line-search heuristics (pp. 2-3, 8-10); unsourced claim that FP is standard in commercial solvers (p. 2); does not cite the co-authors' proximal reading of the pump (pp. 25-27).
writing: Four numbered ideas in the contribution sentence with headline numbers in the introduction (pp. 3-4), goals stated before experiments (p. 17), modest close 'a small incremental step forward' (p. 25).
limits_future: Limit: per-point LPs become substantial with many breakpoints and continuous variables (pp. 8, 25); future: continuous solves at chosen breakpoints only, several directions or tree-like search (p. 25).

method_links.note: shadow design gives every variant the same FP+ iterates; one code base with arms as options; exclusions with reasons; deterioration profile; gaps: CPLEX version not stated, no rival pump variant run

transferable: A breakpoint walk that enumerates all roundings along a segment, one unit change per step (pp. 6-8).
A cheap feasibility direction: the violated rows, weighted by signed distance (p. 11).
Extension with α ∈ [−1, 2], plus projection onto the bounds by filtering breakpoints (pp. 12, 14, 17).
Propagate a variable only after its last change on the line, which gives at most 2|I| propagations (p. 16).

quotes.text: After the integer line search has been executed, FP proceeds as if the execution of the integer line search did not take place. This allows for a fair comparison between the different line searches as the FP trajectory is not altered.
Thus, the performance difference observed earlier is not caused by the choice of end points, but by the difference in number of rounded solutions explored.

title: Benders decomposition without separability: A computational study for capacitated facility location problems
contribution: Computational and algorithmic guidelines for a modern Benders implementation on capacitated and congested facility location with a non-separable slave, plus a simplified generalised Benders cut.
problem_entry: Does Benders help even without separability (p. 1)? Abandoned since Wentges 1996 (p. 3); give guidelines for a modern callback-based implementation for linear multiple-source CFL and congested CFL (pp. 2-5).
key_idea: Project out all allocation variables, aggregate-capacity constraint as global feasibility cut (p. 8); slave with y fixed is much faster after preprocessing (pp. 8-9); blame the root loop, not the cut, and stabilise with an in-out scheme (pp. 9-11).
assumptions: f, g differentiable convex, S a nonempty polytope, X(y) nonempty closed bounded, constraint qualifications (pp. 6-7); multiple-source CFL only (p. 4); congested CFL with quadratic congestion and perspective SOC baseline (pp. 4-6); cap*, GK, i*, p* and 60 congested instances (pp. 14-15, 21-22).
proof_devices: copy-variable cut derivation: y − q = 0 as bounds, cut from reduced costs r* (eqs. 27-31, pp. 7-8)
toy example Φ(y) = |y| showing an LP value function is nonlinear (p. 7)
Lagrangian knapsack recomputation of cut coefficients with assignment duals fixed, valid for any u (pp. 9-10)
experiments: CPLEX 12.6.1, 4 threads, 50,000 s; Benders order of magnitude faster on cap*, beats CPLEX on i* mostly, near-identical root gaps on GK, 210 of 445 p* proven, 45 of 60 congested solved; rivals compared by Linpack-scaled published times; one nondeterministic run, no Kelley ablation (pp. 14-22).
positioning: Rivals Avella-Boccia B&C&P and Görtz-Klose Lagrangian B&B, heuristics Avella et al. and Guastaroba-Speranza (pp. 2-3); revises the dual-degeneracy/cut-selection explanation of slow convergence (pp. 9-10); in-out credited to Ben-Ameur-Neto, Fischetti-Salvagnin, Naoum-Sawaya-Elhedhli and [14] (p. 10).
writing: Question-led hedged abstract (p. 1), one-sentence diagnosis 'the real culprit' (p. 10), tuning restraint stated twice (pp. 17, 22-23), admitted surprise (p. 17), strong closing claims (p. 23).
limits_future: Limits: non-decomposable slave penalises Benders intrinsically (p. 23), last per-mills of gap hard (p. 18), blurring pays only with loose capacities (pp. 11, 16), weak on 1,000 × 1,000 with r = 15 (p. 17); no future work named (pp. 22-23).

method_links.note: primary, joint: diagnosis moves from cut to root loop; in-out query point with Kelley fallback before branching; on 120 GK instances root gaps almost identical to CPLEX's; no Kelley arm, so the loop's share is asserted not measured
stabilisation parameters set by what makes the oracle cheap: separation points close together for a warm-started LP slave
allocation variables projected out and a thin master; the root gain shows where many allocation variables are removed
stock LP solver as slave; plain CPLEX on the compact model is a strong reported baseline solving all i*
what is tested is a fully engineered callback package with defaults overridden, not the smallest code with extras off
spread exploited as a parallel race of perturbed root loops with pooled cuts; no seeds, nondeterministic 4-thread jobs; contradicts the skill's 'single-threaded' blind-spot line for this paper
new method deliberately untuned; both arms same EPGAP on the same machine
a dated lapse: rival methods judged by published times on other hardware and older CPLEX versions, scaled by Linpack

transferable: The copy-variable trick for generalised Benders cuts: y − q = 0 imposed as bounds, with the cut read from their reduced costs (pp. 7-8).
An aggregate-capacity constraint in the master in place of Benders feasibility cuts (p. 8).
For stability, recompute the cut coefficients through Lagrangian knapsacks with the assignment duals fixed (pp. 9-10).
An in-out root loop with a 5 + 5 non-improving-rounds rule and slack purging, whose parameters are set by the slave's warm start (pp. 10-11).
Race the root loop across threads with perturbed parameters, and pool all the cuts (p. 12).
A node give-up rule based on the slave's primal value, and a 50% time cap on fractional separation (p. 13).
Separate every integer candidate in the lazy-constraint callback (p. 13).
Two root restarts that reload the saved cuts as static cuts (p. 13).
Slave tolerances tighter than the master's (1e-9 against 1e-7 and 1e-6) (p. 13).

quotes.text: According to our experience, however, cut selection is important but the cut loop strategy adopted at the root node is the real culprit of inefficiency.
We want to point out that it would be possible to tune our code to speedup convergence for some special cases, but this was not the intention of our computational study.
